extracted.intended_audience: registered patent practitioners (patent attorneys and agents) who practice before the USPTO; Office of Enrollment and Discipline audience
extracted.subtask_description: Final Order summarizing stipulated facts, legal conclusions, and agreed sanctions for USPTO-registered practitioner misconduct; cites specific provisions of 37 C.F.R. and gives examples of conduct violating those rules. Useful as authoritative guidance on practitioner obligations when accepting third‑party referrals, handling client communications, signatures, fees, and responding to OED inquiries.

rubrics_metrics.name: 37 C.F.R. § 11.101 — Competent representation
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioner must provide competent representation to clients; failing to do so violates § 11.101.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example of violation here: signing inventors' names to Oaths, Declarations, and Powers of Attorney and filing them with the USPTO. Surrounding factual context: competence includes proper handling of signature/authorization and ensuring client understanding and consent before filing.

rubrics_metrics.name: 37 C.F.R. § 11.102(a) — Abide by client's decisions concerning objectives
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioner must abide by a client's decisions concerning the objectives of representation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Violations identified: signing clients' names to the Oath, Declaration, and Powers of Attorney and filing those documents; not showing clients key documents related to their applications prior to preparing and filing such documents on their behalf.

rubrics_metrics.name: 37 C.F.R. § 11.103 — Reasonable diligence and promptness
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioner must act with reasonable diligence and promptness in representing a client.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrative misconduct: intentionally failing to timely file completed patent applications because of a fee dispute with a third party (WPM), thereby delaying filings and harming client rights.

rubrics_metrics.name: 37 C.F.R. §§ 11.104(a)(1) and (b) — Explain matters sufficiently for informed decision
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioner must explain matters to the extent reasonably necessary to enable a client to make informed decisions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: failing to explain potential conflicts of interest (e.g., that referrals from a marketing company constituted the majority of the practitioner's business) and failing to disclose material facts about third‑party relationships that affect the representation.

rubrics_metrics.name: 37 C.F.R. § 11.104(a)(2) — Reasonable consultation about means to accomplish objectives
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioner must reasonably consult with the client about the means by which the client's objectives are to be accomplished.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: failing at the outset to consult about the scope of the invention and the most appropriate type of patent application (utility vs. design) for the client's particular invention; allowing third parties to dictate application type without proper client consultation.

rubrics_metrics.name: 37 C.F.R. § 11.104(a)(3) — Keep client reasonably informed about status
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioner must keep the client reasonably informed about the status of a matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: not communicating with clients about key documents related to their applications prior to preparing and filing them, and not promptly informing clients when work on their applications was suspended.

rubrics_metrics.name: 37 C.F.R. § 11.104(b) — Explain matters sufficiently when needed
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioner must explain matters (again emphasized) to enable client informed decisions, including explaining technical/legal terms and the practitioner's actions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Concrete failures here: not personally explaining patent‑law terms in the engagement letter (e.g., 'patent pending,' 'allowance,' 'office action'), not explaining how such terms relate to the client's specific invention, and not promptly explaining he decided not to file completed applications because of a fee dispute and the feasible alternatives available.

rubrics_metrics.name: 37 C.F.R. § 11.107(a) — Informed consent in writing for concurrent conflicts
rubrics_metrics.description: Where the representation involves a concurrent conflict of interest, practitioner must obtain informed consent, confirmed in writing, from the client.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrative violation: representing inventors referred by a marketing company without disclosing that those referrals constituted the majority of the practitioner's business during the relevant period and that the practitioner would be communicating with the marketing company about the type of application to file.

rubrics_metrics.name: 37 C.F.R. §§ 11.303(a)(1), 11.303(a)(3), 11.303(d) — Truthfulness to tribunal / false statements
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioner must not knowingly make false statements of fact to a tribunal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: signing clients' names to Oaths, Declarations, and Powers of Attorney and filing those documents with the USPTO when not properly authorized, which constitutes knowingly making false statements of fact to the Office.

rubrics_metrics.name: 37 C.F.R. § 11.504(c) — Prohibition on third‑party direction of professional judgment
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioner must not permit an entity which recommended, employed, or paid the practitioner to direct or regulate the practitioner's professional judgment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: allowing a marketing/referral company (WPM) to decide the type of application to file for the practitioner's clients; practitioners accepting referrals should avoid allowing the referrer to control professional decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: 37 C.F.R. §§ 11.804(c) and (d) — Dishonesty, fraud, deceit, misrepresentation; prejudicial conduct
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioner must not engage in conduct involving dishonesty, fraud, deceit or misrepresentation, nor conduct that is prejudicial to the administration of justice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples here include signing clients' names to Oaths/Declarations/POAs and filing them, and failing to substantively, in writing, answer OED Requests for Information during an investigation. Such conduct may be charged under § 11.804(c)/(d).

rubrics_metrics.name: 37 C.F.R. § 11.801 — Obligation to respond to OED requests for information (RFIs)
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioner has an ethical obligation to respond to OED Requests for Information during an investigation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Context: OED mailed multiple RFIs; the Final Order notes a 'lack of response' letter and that the practitioner never substantively and in writing responded to the Second or Third RFI. Failure to respond is prejudicial and can be charged under the rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Client engagement and fee‑handling disclosures / informed consent for third‑party payment arrangements
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioner must explain and obtain client understanding/consent regarding engagement terms, patent terminology, fee arrangements (including where a third party holds funds), risks of third‑party payment arrangements, and client responsibilities for payment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples of poor practice: sending standardized engagement letters containing patent terms without personally explaining them; failing to advise clients of risks that the marketing company might not safeguard or remit fees; requiring personal guarantees or equitable liens without ensuring client comprehension; representing that clients attest funds are held in trust by the referrer without independently verifying. Practitioners should disclose risks and alternatives and ensure clients understand and consent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Signature, Oath/Declaration/POA handling and limits on signing for clients
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioner must ensure valid client signatures on Oaths, Declarations, and Powers of Attorney and must not improperly sign a client's name or file documents claiming client signature without proper authorization.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The engagement letter here purported to accept facsimile, typed between hash marks, email signatures and granted a limited power to sign government patent forms; yet the respondent placed clients' electronic signatures on some applications. Guidance: obtain clear, documented client authorization and avoid forging or otherwise placing client signatures without explicit, informed consent; ensure any limited POA is used only within its lawful bounds and accuracy is confirmed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Duty to disclose and avoid allowing referral source to control representation
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioner must disclose relationships with referral sources and avoid permitting the referrer to dictate substantive decisions about the representation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In this case, WPM referred clients, provided questionnaires and drawings, and designated application types; practitioner allowed WPM input on application type and did not disclose the extent of the WPM relationship to clients. Practitioners should disclose referral arrangements, the extent of the referrer's involvement, any payments received from referrers, and obtain clients' informed consent before allowing referrer influence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consequences and conditions for reinstatement after discipline
rubrics_metrics.description: Sanctions for rule violations may include suspension from practice before the USPTO with conditions for reinstatement and probationary requirements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agreed sanction here: 36‑month suspension; permitted to petition for reinstatement after 24 months; conditions of reinstatement include achieving an MPRE score of 85 or better, completing twelve hours of CLE on conflicts/communication/trust accounts/ethics, serving a two‑year probation upon reinstatement, and compliance with USPTO Rules during probation. The Final Order may be published and considered in future disciplinary matters.
